ingredients.item: small yellow or red potatoes, cut into 3 cm chunks
ingredients.preparation: skin on — the skin holds the chunk together through the braise

ingredients.item: toasted sesame seeds ; 1 scallion , sliced; a pinch of gochugaru or sliced chili , optional

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: Oil and garlic in a wide pan over medium until the garlic just turns blond (30 seconds — blond, not brown; browned garlic runs bitter through a sweet braise), potatoes in, stirred to coat, 2 minutes of sizzling together.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the potato edges turn translucent-gold and the pan smells of toasted garlic — the braise's flavor floor just got laid.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Water, soy, corn syrup, and sugar in; stir, lid on, medium-low. Ten minutes at a gentle bubble, stirring once at the halfway mark.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: a paring knife into the largest chunk slides in with no resistance — the potato is cooked, and everything from here is reduction, not cooking. If the knife catches, three more minutes, lid on.

instructions.heading: Lid off, and the reduction — the technique
instructions.action: Lid off, and the reduction — the technique. High-medium now, stirring and turning every 60–90 seconds as the liquid boils down. The braise goes from soupy to syrupy to glaze: the pan's liquids thicken, the sugars caramelize on the turned potato faces, and the potatoes bounce in a slow thick sizzle instead of a boil. Five to six minutes, off the heat the moment the glaze coats and the pan is nearly dry.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: a test chunk: glazed dark at two or three faces, glossy, and it holds its shape but yields to the tooth — the braise has painted it, not dissolved it. Burnt-sugar smell is the one-second warning: off the heat now, not next stir. Sesame oil, seeds, scallion over, off the heat.

storageNotes: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and reheats beautifully (pan, medium, 3 minutes, a splash of water to loosen the glaze) — the make-ahead banchan par excellence, arguably better on day two.
Variations: the same braise on lotus root (#B18) and on quail eggs (#B19); a chili half in the braise for the drinking table; day-after glazed potatoes beside a fried egg is the lunchbox classic.
